text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Prime Minister John Howard has intervened to mend a rift between two senior Coalition Ministers - Environment Minister Robert Hill and Primary Industries and Energy Minister John Anderson - as fallout increases over a national forests peace plan. Howard bcame active in negotiations when Hill angered Anderson by pushing to reserve 10 times as much forest than earlier proposed in the East Gippsland forests agreement which was to have been signed between the Federal and Victorian Governments on Friday. Page 3.

The Transport Workers Union has welcomed the granting of a 15 per cent wage rise to more than 30,000 workers under the New South Wales Transport Industry Award, which the union feels will boost the prospect of an 11 per cent national award wage claim. Howver, the TWU concedes that a hostile Government attitude towards wage claims will become a significant factor in the award of any national wage increase. Page 4.

Victorian Opposition leader John Brumby is expected to be re-elected unopposed in the tough position as Premier Jeff Kennett's adversary at a special ALP Caucus meeting today, after a factional deal strengthened the hand of his right-wing Labor Unity facton. The deal represents a significant shift within the Victorian Labor Party as it replaces a previous factional power-sharing agreement between Labor Unity and the Socialist Left, the Victorian ALP's main faction. Page 5.

Defence Minister Ian McLachlan has pushed forward in plans to shift Australia's defence policy toward a more assertive forward military force projection to meet future security threats in the post-Cold War Asia-Pacific region. The new policy, although stil under development and expected to be unveiled next year, is believed to propose that Australia deploy forces into possible future Asia-Pacific trouble spots, especially if there were potential threats. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

A survey by The Australian of 15 leading non-government schools in Australia has found the costs of enrolling students at private schools in Australia will rise in 1997, with many fees set to increase by up to 9.5 per cent to cover pay increases for teachers, and the demand for state-of-the-art technology. Page 1.

The Balderson family, who have been the last remaining family living at The Monument, an outback town 150 kilometres south of Mt Isa, say this will be their last Christmas in the town. Mr Balderson has been the caretaker of the settlement for Western Minng Corp while it waited to reactivate a phosphate mine 16 kilometres away. However, when work begins on the A$650 million mine next year, workers will fly in for two weeks and out for one, leaving their families well away from The Monument. Page 1

The High Court will today hand down its decision in the case of the Wik claim over 35,000 square kilometres of land in Cape York. The decision will impact the affect of native title over pastoral leases in Queensland and Western Australia. The claim itslf covers pastoral leases and the bauxite mining leases of aluminium producer Comalco Ltd at Weipa. Page 1.

Victorian Opposition Leader John Brumby looks set to replace his deputy, Demetri Dollis, with the high-profile health spokesperson John Thwaites at a Victorian ALP Caucus meeting this morning. The move will kickstart a purge by Brumby of the party's longserving MPs. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has called on Prime Minister John Howard and Federal Opposition Leader Kim Beazley to commit themselves to sweeping tax reform, including some form of a consumption tax, straight after the next election. Kennett acknowledges that Howard is unable to introduce any kind of reform in his first term due to a promise to voters, but believes strong political leadership on the issue is required. Page 1.

Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer has stated it is "disappointing" that China has moved to install a shadow administration in Hong Kong six months before it takes over the territory next year, but has stopped short of joining the United States and Britain in condemning the move. Page 1.

New South Wales Court of Appeal president Keith Mason, QC, has attacked the Federal Government's large funding cuts to legal aid, claiming the cuts put judges at risk of making expensive mistakes. Mason added that court cases where defendants defend themelves because of the cuts will take longer. Page 1.

Federal Opposition legal affairs spokesman Nick Bolkus said yesterday the Federal Government should intervene in the case of two Aboriginal children being detained over Christmas for allegedly spitting at Independent MP Pauline Hanson in her electorate ofice. Bolkus believes the penalty is unfair, claiming it is these kinds of sentences that lead to deaths in custody. Page 3.
THE AGE

The Federal Government is seeking urgent talks with the Queensland Government following the national outcry over yesterday's jailing of two Aboriginal children for allegedly spitting at controversial MP Pauline Hanson. Federal Attorney-General Daryl Willims indicated last night that he wanted urgent talks with the State's Justice Minister over the two brothers, aged 11 and 12, remaining in custody until the 30 of January. Page A1.

Victoria's Socialist Left MPs have rejected an all-out factional war which has previously plagued the party and endorsed Opposition Leader John Brumby for re-election in his position. At a Caucus meeting on the weekend, Brumby called for a spill of all ledership and shadow Cabinet positions and stands to have his job reconfirmed in today's party election as the Socialist Left faction decided not to stand a candidate against him. Page A1.

Governments, indigenous groups and farmers are hoping today's High Court ruling on the Wik native title claim will decide if Aboriginal land rights survive the granting of a pastoral lease. The case is the outstanding issue from the 1992 Mabo decision, which first recognised native title on Murray Island, and should decide the future of up to 40 per cent of Australian land under pastoral leases. Page A1.

Former Prime Minister Paul Keating has pulled out of a deal with Channel 4 in England which would have seen him in a pro-republican broadcast to coincide with the Queen's traditional Christmas broadcast. The Sunday Times in England reports that Keating pulled out of the deal because he believed he had no right to urge Britain to depose the Queen as head of state. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
